description:
Wesam Saad explains the place of gospel preaching in the order of salvation. Resuming the previous meeting’s unfinished question, he distinguishes the preacher’s outward invitation from God’s life-giving holy calling. Romans 10 supplies the sequence of preaching, hearing, believing and calling on the Lord. He then turns to the word of truth in James and the enduring preached word in 1 Peter to argue that gospel proclamation also precedes regeneration. The purpose is more than remembering a diagram: listeners should locate the teaching in Scripture and be able to explain its basis, rather than depend on a persuasive teacher or an isolated theological illustration.

Ezekiel’s vision of the dry bones provides the main extended illustration. Saad emphasises that the prophet addresses the bones while relying on God to bring life. He applies this to perseverance in evangelism, even when a person appears resistant, without promising any particular hearer’s conversion. Questions address Matthew 7:6, prayer for unbelievers and the relationship between preaching and God’s action. Saad encourages prayer together with active gospel witness, not replacing either with the other. He also acknowledges the vision’s setting in Israel’s promised renewal before explaining its application within his account of salvation. The following sessions are explicitly directed towards TULIP.

questions.question: What unfinished question does this session answer?
questions.answer: It asks where the preacher’s external call belongs in the saving sequence and how it differs from God’s holy calling. Saad argues that gospel proclamation is the appointed means preceding the divine work of regeneration and the person’s believing. He develops this from passages rather than leaving the diagram as an unsupported assertion.

questions.question: How does he use Romans 10 to explain gospel hearing?
questions.answer: Saad follows Paul’s rhetorical questions from preaching to hearing, believing and calling on the Lord for salvation. He reasons that hearing the gospel must precede believing it, and preaching must make that hearing possible. He then seeks further passages to establish where proclamation belongs relative to regeneration.

questions.question: How do James and 1 Peter support the argument?
questions.answer: The word of truth is presented as the means by which God brings people forth, while 1 Peter connects new birth with the enduring word preached to the hearers. Saad takes these passages as evidence that the gospel is not merely information supplied after conversion but a means through which God gives new life.

questions.question: What does the dry-bones vision illustrate?
questions.answer: Saad follows the prophet’s proclamation, the formation of bodies and the giving of breath in Ezekiel 37. The bones cannot supply their own life, and the prophet cannot create it by his speaking skill. He uses the vision to illustrate God giving life through the proclaimed word.

questions.question: Why does divine initiative encourage preaching rather than make it unnecessary?
questions.answer: In Saad’s explanation, God brings life through the preaching of the word rather than bypassing it. The speaker therefore has a real task without becoming the source of regeneration. Since the preacher does not know whom God will save, apparent resistance does not make that task pointless.

questions.question: Where should the evangelist’s confidence rest?
questions.answer: Saad directs confidence towards God’s power to give life, rather than the hearer’s apparent softness or the speaker’s ability to out-argue someone. This supports perseverance through rejection. It does not guarantee a particular conversion or turn indifference towards the hearer into the goal of evangelism.

questions.question: Why does he warn against relying only on the dead-in-sin illustration?
questions.answer: Saad notes that unbelievers can perform outwardly helpful acts, so an illustration about a corpse cannot by itself settle every question about spiritual inability. He urges listeners to establish the order and meaning from Scripture first, then use concepts and illustrations in support rather than as the foundation.

questions.question: Does he treat Matthew 7:6 as a general ban on witnessing to resistant sinners?
questions.answer: No. Saad argues against reading the saying as a general prohibition on preaching the gospel to sinners or Gentiles. He refers listeners to a longer written explanation and does not fully develop it during this session.

questions.question: How should prayer and gospel witness relate?
questions.answer: Saad commends praying for unbelievers and for God to give life, while also praying that the gospel reaches them. He challenges prayer that becomes a substitute for speaking the gospel and explicitly calls for more preaching rather than less prayer.

questions.question: How does he address Ezekiel’s original setting and the wider application?
questions.answer: Saad identifies Israel’s future renewal within the new-covenant context as the vision’s specific setting. He then connects its life-giving pattern with the New Testament passages on new birth through the word. A further question about Old Testament salvation is deferred rather than fully answered here.
